introduction-the-shared-secret-problem.core: Services verifying JWTs signed with a shared HMAC secret (HS256) must all hold the same secret, which can also mint tokens, so any compromised service can forge tokens for all, and rotation means updating every service at once. Asymmetric signing (RS256, ES256, EdDSA) fixes that: only the issuer holds the private key, and verifiers fetch public keys. A JWKS is the standard JSON document publishing those public keys.

first_principles.problem: A compromised low-value microservice uses the shared HS256 secret to mint admin tokens for every API.
truths: Keys must be discoverable and rotatable.

analogy.title: A wax seal vs a shared stamp
analogy.story: With one shared stamp, anyone holding it can forge decrees; with a seal only the king holds, everyone can check against a public specimen.
analogy.breaks: Specimens are posted once; JWKS rotates keys regularly.

example.title: Blast radius
flow: HS256: 40 services hold secret → any can forge
ES256: issuer holds private key in KMS
Compromised service can verify, not forge

check.q: Why is HS256 risky in a microservices architecture?
check.a: Every verifying service holds the secret that can also sign tokens, so compromising any one allows forging tokens for all.

what-is-a-jwks.core: A JSON Web Key Set (RFC 7517) is a JSON object with a keys array. Each JWK has kty (RSA or EC or OKP), kid (key ID), use (sig) or key_ops, alg (RS256, ES256), and the public parameters (n and e for RSA; crv, x and y for EC). Identity providers publish it at a jwks_uri advertised in OIDC discovery (/.well-known/openid-configuration). Verifiers read a JWT's header kid, select the matching key and verify the signature.

first_principles.problem: Engineers hardcode a PEM public key in every service and break everything when the IdP rotates keys.

analogy.title: A public directory of seal specimens
analogy.story: Each specimen has a number; a document says which seal number was used, so you look up that one.
analogy.breaks: Directories change rarely; JWKS rotates on schedule.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Verifiers pick key by kid automatically.

check.q: How does a verifier know which JWKS key to use for a JWT?
check.a: It reads the kid in the JWT header and selects the key with the matching kid from the JWKS.

key-rotation-zero-downtime-security.core: Rotate signing keys without breaking verification. (1) Generate the new key and publish its public half in the JWKS alongside the old one; wait at least the verifiers' cache TTL. (2) Switch signing to the new key, so new tokens carry the new kid. (3) Keep the old public key until all tokens it signed have expired (the maximum token lifetime). (4) Remove the old key. Emergency rotation after compromise removes the old key immediately and accepts forced re-login.

first_principles.problem: An IdP switches signing keys and removes the old one at the same moment, invalidating every active session.

analogy.title: Changing the locks with a grace period
analogy.story: Hand out new keys first, switch the lock to accept both, and only later stop accepting the old key.
analogy.breaks: Locks don't cache; verifiers do, so timing matters.

example.title: Rotation timeline
flow: Day 0: add kid 2026-10-a to JWKS (old 2026-07-b still signs)

check.q: Why must a new signing key be published in the JWKS before it's used to sign tokens?
check.a: Verifiers cache the JWKS; publishing first ensures they've fetched the new key before tokens signed with it arrive.

caching-strategies-dont-dos-your-own-aut.core: Fetching the JWKS on every request adds latency and can overwhelm the IdP. Cache it in memory, respecting Cache-Control or a sensible TTL (minutes to hours). On an unknown kid, refetch once, rate-limited, to pick up newly rotated keys, then reject if still unknown. Serve stale keys if the IdP is briefly unavailable, and share caches across workers. Mature libraries (jose, jwks-rsa, go-oidc) implement this correctly.

first_principles.problem: Each API pod fetches the JWKS on every request, and a traffic spike takes down the auth server.

analogy.title: Keeping a copy of the directory at reception
analogy.story: You check your copy, and only call head office for an update when you see a seal number you don't recognise.
analogy.breaks: Receptions don't get spammed; unrate-limited refetches can DoS the IdP.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One fetch per 10 min per pod; rotation handled.

check.q: Why rate-limit JWKS refetches triggered by unknown kids?
check.a: Attackers could send tokens with random kids to force constant refetches, overloading the auth server.

security-considerations-and-attack-vecto.core: Common JWT and JWKS attacks: alg: none acceptance; algorithm confusion (an RS256 public key used as an HS256 secret); jku or x5u header injection (pointing verifiers at an attacker's key set); kid injection (path traversal or SQL in kid lookups); missing iss, aud or exp checks; overly long lifetimes; and tokens in URLs or logs. Defences: pin allowed algorithms, fetch JWKS only from a configured URL, validate all claims, keep tokens short-lived and use proven libraries.

first_principles.problem: An API accepts a token whose header sets jku to an attacker-hosted JWKS, so attacker-signed tokens validate.
derivation: Use **short TTLs** and keep tokens out of logs.

analogy.title: A forged letter that tells you where to verify its seal
analogy.story: A forger includes a note saying 'check my seal against this specimen', and the specimen is also forged.
analogy.breaks: Clerks might notice odd notes; code follows headers unless told not to.

code.text:
import jwt
jwks = jwt.PyJWKClient("https://login.acme.com/.well-known/jwks.json")   # fixed URL
key = jwks.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token).key
claims = jwt.decode(token, key,
    algorithms=["ES256"],                        # never derived from header
    audience="https://api.acme.com",
    issuer="https://login.acme.com",
    options={"require": ["exp", "iat", "sub"]})

check.q: What is the JWT algorithm confusion attack?
check.a: Tricking a verifier into treating an RSA public key as an HMAC secret (switching alg to HS256), letting attackers forge tokens using the public key.
